title: How Mild Preferences Can Sort a Whole City: Exploring Schelling's Segregation Model

source.title: Understanding the social context of the Schelling segregation model
source.authors: William A V Clark, Mark Fossett

intro.summary: This lesson draws on four sources about Thomas Schelling's model of segregation. The sources are a Wikipedia overview, Clark and Fossett's 2008 review linking the model to survey data, Gauvin and colleagues' physics-style map of the model's behaviour, and Rogers and McKane's framework that unites its many variants. Together they ask how a city can become highly segregated when each household holds only a mild preference for similar neighbours. Simulations and mathematics show that segregation appears once the share of like neighbours people want passes a threshold (about one third for two equal groups, and about a group's own share of the city in Clark and Fossett's three-group runs), that it appears sharply rather than gradually, and that this holds across many model versions. The main limitation is that these are deliberately simplified models: they show that preferences can produce segregation, not that they do in real cities, and the sources stress that non-experimental data cannot separate the effects of preferences from those of housing discrimination; the sources also disagree on how much the physics analogies (Ising and spin models) add compared with the model's social content. The lesson does not cover the Ising and statistical-mechanics mapping, entropy measures, game-theoretic 'Schelling games', or extensions with income and housing prices, which are good follow-up topics.
background: Residential segregation means different groups living in separate neighbourhoods, even within one city.
An agent-based model is a computer simulation in which many simple 'agents' (here, households) each follow their own small rule, and we watch what pattern the whole group makes.
Schelling first ran his model by hand in the 1970s, moving coins on a checkerboard, long before such simulations were common.
Social scientists have long debated how much segregation comes from discrimination and how much comes from people's own choices about neighbours.
intro.aha: Households that would happily live as a one-third minority among their neighbours still end up in a city where most people's neighbours are just like them: the city becomes far more segregated than anyone asked for.

primer.heading: The question
primer.body: Many cities are split into neighbourhoods where one group dominates. One explanation is discrimination: people are kept out. Schelling asked a different question. Could ordinary, fairly mild preferences, such as 'I'd like at least some neighbours like me', sort a city on their own, even with no one being forced?
primer.quote: Is it reasonable to entertain the hypothesis that social distance and preference dynamics could generate and sustain significant levels of segregation in the absence of discrimination
primer.quote_where: Preferences, Tolerance, and the Basis of Simulation Models

primer.heading: What they did
primer.body: Schelling imagined a checkerboard. Each square is a home, and each home is empty or holds a household from one of two groups. A household looks at its eight surrounding squares. If too few of those neighbours are from its own group, it is unhappy and moves to an empty square. Later researchers ran this on computers, varied the rules, measured how segregated the board becomes, added survey data on real preferences, and wrote equations for it. The versions differ in their details: one source describes Schelling's rule as wanting half or more like neighbours, others as wanting at least one third.
primer.quote: It posited that an agent, a model representation of a household that could be white or black, preferred to be on a square on a checkerboard in which half or more of the eight adjacent neighbors were of a similar color.

primer.heading: What they found
primer.body: A board that starts well mixed sorts itself into large one-group areas, even when every household would be content as a minority in its neighbourhood. The change is not gradual. Below a certain level of pickiness the city stays mixed, and just above it the city segregates strongly; asking for even more like neighbours adds little. In Clark and Fossett's three-group simulations, the jump came when the share of like neighbours people wanted rose past their group's share of the city. Gauvin and colleagues found that the number of empty homes also matters: the model can be frozen, segregated or mixed. Rogers and McKane showed that very different versions of the model segregate along the same early curve.
primer.quote: Thus, high levels of segregation emerge when targets for same-group contact shift from 20% to 40%.

primer.heading: Why it matters, and its limits
primer.body: If mild preferences alone can segregate a city, then removing discrimination may not by itself produce integration, and the policy tools for the two causes are very different. But a model shows what is possible, not what actually happened. Real cities have many forces acting at once, and observational data cannot cleanly separate the effects of preferences from those of discrimination. The authors argue that both probably work together.
primer.quote: Because neither group can establish empirically grounded evaluations of the effects of either preferences or discrimination, recent work has focused on the logical standing of explanations based on social distance
primer.quote_where: Preferences, Tolerance, and the Basis of Simulation Models

primer.heading: Where the sources disagree
primer.body: Physicists have noticed that the model behaves like models of magnets and alloys, and they borrow their tools to map its behaviour. Clark and Fossett grant that this is interesting, but they argue that the model's real value lies in how household choices play out in society. Rogers and McKane add that the many versions of the model make the literature fragmented, which is why they propose a single framework.
primer.quote: That the Schelling model has a physical analogue is interesting and theoretically illuminating is without question, but it is the social content of the Schelling model that gives it its power and importance.

concepts.title: A city of simple rules
concepts.idea: Each household follows one rule (if too few neighbours are like me, move to an empty home), and the computer applies that rule to everyone, round after round.

predict.question: Picture the same rule in a city where every single home is taken: no empty homes at all. Households want about a third of their neighbours to be like them. After 40 rounds, what do you expect?
options: The households that started out unhappy are still unhappy, and nothing has changed
Everyone ends up content, because the computer keeps applying the rule
Unhappy households swap homes with each other until they are content
Unhappy households lower what they want until they are content
why: Right: the rule's only action is moving into an empty home. With none available, an unhappy household has nowhere to go, so the grid stays as it began.
Repeating the rule only helps if it can do something. Here the rule's one action, moving to an empty home, is impossible, so more rounds change nothing.
Swapping is a different rule. Some variants allow it, but the rule here only lets a household move into an empty home, and there are none.
In this rule what a household wants is fixed. Only where it lives can change, and here even that is blocked.

The smallest share of like neighbours a household accepts before it decides to move; Wikipedia writes it B_a

feedback.correct: Yes. The rule has exactly one action, moving into an empty home. Take away the empty homes and the rule can do nothing, however many rounds the computer runs.
feedback.incorrect: It is tempting to think repeating the rule always fixes things. But the rule only says 'if unhappy, move to an empty home'. With no empty homes, no household can act, so the city stays exactly as it started.

steps.say: Start gentle: each household wants only 20% of its neighbours to be like it, and the computer runs a single round.
Each household looks only at the eight homes touching it, its Moore neighbourhood. Empty homes there don't count either way.
It works out what share of those occupied neighbours are like it. If that share is below the wanted share, its satisfaction threshold, the household is unhappy and moves to a random empty home.
One round means every household checks once. A move can land a household somewhere no better, so a single round may not settle everyone. Check the unhappy box.
Let the computer repeat the rule. Each round, everyone checks again, and the unhappy ones move again.
With modest wants, the unhappy share falls to about zero, and the computer stops early. See how few rounds it needed.
Now make households picky: each wants 80% of its neighbours like it. Same rule, same city.
Now many cannot find a home that pleases them. The computer uses every round and still leaves a big share unhappy. One simple rule, applied over and over, gives very different cities.

understand.explanation: Schelling's model gives every household the same single rule. Look at the occupied homes around you, and if too small a share are like you, move to an empty home. The computer applies that rule to everyone, then does it again, round after round, until everyone is content or it is told to stop. Schelling first did this by hand, moving pawns on a chessboard. The sources describe his setting differently: one says households wanted half or more of their neighbours alike, another says at least a third. The rule is the same; only the number differs. The model is deliberately bare: no prices, no discrimination, no other reasons to move, so it can show only what this one rule can do on its own.
understand.quote: It posited that an agent, a model representation of a household that could be white or black, preferred to be on a square on a checkerboard in which half or more of the eight adjacent neighbors were of a similar color.

equation.text: ,  where B = like neighbours ÷ occupied neighbours

connect.caption: This is the rule as Wikipedia writes it. B_{a} (blue) is the wanted share, the satisfaction threshold set by the first slider. B is the share of a household's occupied neighbours that are like it; empty homes are ignored. If B falls below B_{a}, the household moves; otherwise it stays.

concepts.recap: One rule for everyone: count your like neighbours, and move if there are too few. The computer repeats it round after round, and how picky the rule is decides whether the city settles.

concepts.title: Measuring how sorted a city is
concepts.idea: Segregation can be measured as the average share of a household's neighbours who are from its own group: about 50% in a randomly mixed two-group city, rising toward 100% as the city sorts.

predict.question: A different two-group city, also with equal groups, is simulated for many rounds. At the end, its average share of same-group neighbours reads 51%. What does that tell you?
options: The city is about as mixed as if households had been placed at random
About half of the households live in segregated areas
About half of the households are still unhappy
The city is moderately segregated, halfway to complete sorting
why: Right: with two equal groups placed at random, each neighbour is close to a coin flip, so about 50% is the starting level. A reading of 51% means almost no sorting has happened.

Tempting, because 51% sounds like 'half the city'. But the measure is an average over every household. It does not split households into segregated and not segregated, and 50% is exactly what pure chance gives.

Tempting, because both numbers are shares of households. But happiness is a separate output. A city can read near 50% with everyone content (when nobody cares) or with many unhappy (when nobody can settle).
Tempting if you read the scale as running from 0% to 100%. For two equal groups, though, the measure starts near 50% when nothing has sorted. Halfway to complete sorting would be about 75%, not 51%.

terms.means: The value a measure takes when households are placed purely at random: here about 50% for two equal groups
The share of neighbour pairs that are from different groups; it is roughly 100% minus the same-group share

model.title: The same small city, now with a score for how sorted it is
model.note: Teaching model: the same 20×20 grid as before, with two equal groups and 10% of homes empty. Only unhappy households move, and each jumps to a random empty home. The score looks at every household, takes the share of its occupied neighbouring homes (up to eight) that hold its own group, and averages that share over the city; empty homes are ignored. Rogers and McKane's interface density counts neighbour pairs rather than households, so 100% minus the score is close to their measure but not identical. Numbers are illustrative, not the sources' data.

feedback.correct: Yes. For two equal groups, about 50% is the random baseline: the level chance alone produces. A reading of 51% means the city has barely sorted at all.
feedback.incorrect: You probably read 51% on a scale where 0% means 'not sorted'. For two equal groups, though, pure chance already gives about 50%. The score climbs from there toward 100% as like settles beside like, so 51% means almost no sorting.

steps.say: Begin with households that don't care at all, and give them all 60 rounds. Nobody is ever unhappy, so nobody moves.
The city is just as it was dealt out: at random. Look at the score. It sits close to 50%.
Why half? With two equal groups placed at random, each neighbour is close to a coin flip: equally likely to be either colour. This chance level is called the random baseline.
Now let households want at least 30% like neighbours, but stop after a single round. The unhappy ones have made one move each, and the score has already risen above the baseline.
Give them 10 rounds. Unhappy households keep moving, and the score climbs further.
Its mirror image falls at the same time. Researchers call the share of neighbour pairs that come from different groups the interface density. It starts near one half and drops as the city sorts.
Now run all 60 rounds. Same wish, more time to move. The same-group share has climbed well above half, and clumps of one colour are easy to see on the grid.

understand.explanation: The measure looks at each household, finds the share of its occupied neighbouring homes that hold its own group, and averages that share over the whole city. When two equal groups are placed at random, each neighbour is close to a coin flip, so the average starts near 50%: the random baseline. As unhappy households move, like settles beside like, so the average climbs toward 100% and its mirror image, the interface density, falls toward 0. Rogers and McKane tracked interface density over time in five quite different versions of Schelling's model, all starting from random arrangements. Early on, all five followed one shared curve down. This is one way to measure sorting, not the only one: Gauvin and colleagues measure the size of single-colour clusters instead, and Schelling warned that such numbers describe an artificial checkerboard, not a real city.
understand.quote: If such a local measurement is taken at each site and the result averaged over the whole network, one obtains an aggregate measure for the level of segregation in the system.

equation.text: = (edges between agents of opposite types) ÷ (edges between agents of any type),

connect.caption: The first part is Rogers and McKane's equation (3) for the interface density x. An 'edge' is a pair of next-door homes, both occupied. x matches the other-group share in the model. The second part is this model's reading: the same-group share is about 1 − x. It is only approximately equal because the model averages household by household, while x counts neighbour pairs.

concepts.recap: Average the share of each household's neighbours who are its own group: about 50% means randomly mixed (for two equal groups), and climbing toward 100% means the city is sorting.

activities.title: Scoring one household, then a whole city

steps.text: Pick one household. Around it are eight homes: 5 hold its own group, 2 hold the other group, and 1 is empty.
Empty homes are ignored, so only 7 neighbours count.
Its same-group share is 5 out of 7.
A second household has 3 of its own group among 8 occupied neighbours.
Do this for every household in the city and take the average. That single number is the city's score.
In a city of two equal groups placed at random, each neighbour is about a coin flip, so these shares scatter around one half.

activities.takeaway: One household's share can be high or low by luck. The city's average is what tells you whether like has gathered with like beyond what chance gives.

activities.question: Now imagine a made-up city where one group is 80% of households and the other is 20%, all placed at random. For a household in the smaller group, about what share of its neighbours would be its own group?
activities.explanation: At random, each neighbour is a draw from the whole city, and 20% of the city is the smaller group, so its random baseline is about 20%. A household in the larger group would see about 80%. The 50% baseline holds only when the two groups are equal. So before you call a reading 'sorted', always compare it with what chance gives for that city.

concepts.title: One move tips two neighbourhoods
concepts.idea: When an unhappy household moves, its old neighbourhood loses one of its group and its new neighbourhood gains one, which can make other households unhappy and set off further moves.

terms.means: A chain in which the result of one step causes more of the same step, which causes more again
A run of moves in which each move triggers the next, like falling dominoes

concepts.recap: A move changes the mix in two places at once, so one household's choice can make others unhappy and keep the moving going.

understand.explanation: On the street you just watched, one household's move changed the mix of two blocks at once. Its old block lost one of its group, so the rest of that group there were more outnumbered. Its new block gained one, so the other group there were more outnumbered. When that pushes someone below the share they want, they move too, and their move changes two more blocks. A loop like this, where each step causes more of the same step, is called a feedback loop, and the run of moves it sets off is called a cascade. Clark and Fossett describe this loop in Schelling-style simulations, and Gauvin and colleagues note that one move can cost the old and new neighbours more than it gains the mover. This is how the model's rules behave: it shows how mild preferences could snowball, not proof that real households move this way.
understand.quote: However, their moves to satisfy this objective—that is, moving from an area where their group is in the minority to one where it is at least half—change the ethnic mix in both locations in a way that precipitates further movement. The neighborhood they leave becomes less attractive to members of their group and the neighborhood they enter becomes less attractive to members of the other group.
understand.quote_where: Section 'Preferences, Tolerance, and the Basis of Simulation Models'

activities.prompt: Here is a made-up town with two blocks, Ash and Birch. Each has 10 homes. Some households are Blue and some are Orange. Each household follows one rule: it stays content if its colour makes up at least half of its block, counting itself. If its colour drops below half, it is unhappy and moves to the other block. This is far simpler than Schelling's grid, where each home has eight neighbours. Reveal the snapshots one at a time and watch who becomes unhappy.

stages.label: Start
stages.text: Ash: 3 Blue, 3 Orange, 4 empty homes. Every household there is content, because each colour is exactly half. Birch: 3 Blue, 4 Orange, 3 empty homes. The Oranges are 4 of 7 (57%), so they are content. The Blues are 3 of 7 (43%), so all three Blues in Birch are unhappy.

stages.label: One move
stages.text: One unhappy Blue leaves Birch for Ash. Ash is now 4 Blue and 3 Orange, so the Oranges in Ash are 3 of 7 (43%). All three Ash Oranges, content a moment ago, are now unhappy. Birch is now 2 Blue and 4 Orange, so the two Blues left behind are 2 of 6 (33%): even more outnumbered than before.

stages.label: The reply
stages.text: One unhappy Orange leaves Ash for Birch. Ash is now 4 Blue and 2 Orange, so the two remaining Oranges are 33%: worse off. Birch is now 2 Blue and 5 Orange, so the two Blues there are 2 of 7 (29%): worse off again. Each move made the next one more likely.

stages.label: The end
stages.text: Everyone who is outnumbered keeps moving. Finally Ash holds 6 Blue and no Orange, and Birch holds 7 Orange and no Blue. Every household is content, and the two blocks are completely sorted by colour.

stages.label: Look back
stages.text: Ash began as a 50/50 block where nobody wanted to leave. Nobody in Ash changed their rule. Ash fell apart only because of moves that started in Birch.

activities.takeaway: A single move changed two blocks at once: the block it left and the block it entered. Each change pushed other households below the share they wanted, so they moved too.

activities.prompt: Put the steps of the loop you watched in order, starting from one unhappy household.
items: A household finds that its group is below the share it wants nearby, so it becomes unhappy
It moves to a place where its group makes up a bigger share
The mix changes in both places: the old place has one fewer of its group, and the new place has one more
Some other households, in the old place or the new one, now fall below the share they want
Those households move too, and the loop starts again
activities.explanation: The loop closes because the last step feeds back into the first: the households that become unhappy are the next ones to move. The third step is the key one. A move never touches just one neighbourhood; it changes the mix where the household leaves and where it arrives. That is why Clark and Fossett say these moves 'precipitate further movement'.
hints: Start with the feeling that makes someone want to move, and end with the step that brings you back to the start.
The change in the mix has to happen before anyone else becomes unhappy.

activities.question: In the town of Ash and Birch, every Orange household in Ash was content at the start, yet they all left. What drove them out?

options.text: A Blue household arrived from Birch, which pushed the Orange share in Ash below half
options.feedback: Right. The Ash Oranges kept the same rule throughout. The arrival changed the mix of their block, which put them below the share they wanted. That is the 'new neighbourhood' half of the loop.

options.text: The Ash Oranges became less tolerant over time
options.feedback: Not in this model. Every household kept the same rule from start to finish. What changed was the block around them, not their preference. The cascade needs no change of heart, only moves that change the mix.

options.text: Someone forced them out of Ash
options.feedback: Nothing in these rules forces anyone to move. Each household moves only by its own choice. Clark and Fossett stress that such voluntary moves are a different thing from discrimination, though in real cities both can act together.

options.text: Ash was badly mixed from the start, so it was always going to sort
options.feedback: Ash started as a 50/50 block where everyone was content and nobody wanted to leave. It sorted only after moves that began in Birch reached it. That is the point of the loop: a stable block can be tipped from outside.

hints: Did any household's rule change during the story?
Look at the 'One move' snapshot: what happened to Ash's mix?

activities.question: A new case: in another made-up town, households are content as long as their colour makes up at least 20% of their block. One Blue household moves into a block of 3 Blue and 3 Orange. Will a cascade start?

options.text: No. The Oranges become 3 of 7 (43%), still above 20%, so nobody else becomes unhappy and the chain stops
options.feedback: Right. A move changes two places, but the loop only continues if that change pushes someone below the share they want. Here the Oranges are still well above 20%, so nobody else moves. The chain needs each step to tip someone over their limit.

options.text: Yes. Every move changes the mix in two places, so a chain always follows
options.feedback: Every move does change the mix in two places, but a change only matters if it pushes someone below the share they want. At a 20% limit, one new arrival leaves the Oranges at 43%, still content. A changed mix is not enough on its own to keep the chain going.

options.text: Yes, but only the Blues will move, because their block got more crowded
options.feedback: In this model the rule is about the share of your own colour, not about crowding. The Blues gained a member, which only makes them more content. Nobody's share falls below 20%, so nobody moves.

hints: Work out the Orange share after the Blue household arrives.
Compare that share with the 20% the households want.

concepts.title: The tipping point near one third
concepts.idea: As the share of like neighbours each household wants rises past about one third, the city flips sharply from staying mixed to segregating strongly; it does not change gradually.

predict.question: Two made-up towns each have two equal-sized groups. In Town A, the share of like neighbours households want rises from 20% to 40%. In Town B, it rises from 50% to 70%. Both wishes rose by 20 points. According to the sources' models, which town's sorting rises more?
options: Town A
Town B
Both rise by about the same amount
Neither changes much
why: Correct: Town A's change crosses the threshold near one third, where the city flips from mixed to strongly sorted. Town B was already past it, and in the sources extra wishes there add little.
It is tempting to think stronger wishes always do more harm. Town B was already past the threshold and already sorted, so it has little room left to change.
This is the 'gradual dial' picture: equal steps in the wish give equal steps in sorting. The sources find a jump near the threshold and small changes beyond it.
Town B does change little, but Town A crosses the threshold, and its sorting leaps.

terms.means: The setting where a small change in individual wishes flips the whole city from one pattern (mixed) to another (sorted)
The share of like neighbours wanted at which the tipping point happens; Schelling found it near one third for two equal groups

model.title: The same small city, now with a score for how sorted it is
model.note: Teaching model: the same 20×20 grid as before, with two equal groups and 10% of homes empty. Only unhappy households move, and each jumps to a random empty home. Schelling moved them to the nearest home that would satisfy them, and Gauvin and colleagues let anyone move, but only to a satisfying home. The score averages, over all households, the share of occupied neighbouring homes (up to eight) that hold the household's own group. Because a household has at most eight neighbours, only certain wishes really differ: wanting 30% and wanting 35% often mean the same thing, at least 3 like neighbours out of 8. On this small grid with random moves, the score already rises somewhat at low wishes, so the jump is softer than in the sources' models. Where the jump falls also depends on the rules: it is near one third in Schelling's classic set-up and near one quarter in Gauvin and colleagues' variant. At very high wishes, households in this simplified model can keep moving without settling; this concept does not look at that range. Numbers are illustrative, not the sources' data.

Watch the sorting score. It stays fairly close to the random mix only while the wish is small.

feedback.correct: Right. In the sources' models, sorting is not a dial that turns smoothly with the wish. The big change happens when the wish crosses the threshold near one third. Town A crosses it; Town B was already past it.
feedback.incorrect: You probably pictured sorting rising steadily with how much people want. In the sources' models it stays low at small wishes, jumps near the threshold, and then changes little. So a 20-point rise that crosses the threshold matters far more than one that starts beyond it.

steps.say: Start with nobody caring who lives next door. No one is unhappy, no one moves, and the score sits at the random baseline of about 50%.
Now each household wants a fifth of its neighbours to be like it. A few households move, and the score rises somewhat above 50%. The grid still looks well mixed.
A quarter. Watch the score and the grid: some sorting, but no large one-colour areas yet.
Now just past one third. Many more households start out unhappy, their moves trigger other moves, and one-colour patches spread across the grid.

When a small change in wishes flips the whole city, that is a tipping point. Schelling found this segregation threshold near one third for two equal groups. Here the flip is softer than in his models.
Now ask for half. Compare how much the score changes here with how much it changed around one third.
Go back to just past one third. Nobody here asked to be in the majority, yet the city is clearly sorted. A modest wish was enough.

understand.explanation: At low wishes, few households are unhappy, so the city stays fairly mixed. Once the wish nears and passes about one third, many households start out unhappy at once. Their moves set off further moves, and the city sorts strongly. In the sources, asking for more past that point adds comparatively little. Schelling found this threshold near one third for two equal groups. Clark and Fossett's three-group simulations found high segregation appearing when targets rose from 20% to 40%, with little extra from higher targets, and Gauvin and colleagues found sharp jumps in their own variant. Where the jump falls, and how sharp it looks, depends on the rules: in Gauvin's variant it sits nearer one quarter, and on this small grid with random moves it is softer. These are simulations of imagined cities, not measurements of real ones.
understand.quote: Perhaps surprising to some, raising targets for same-group contact to even higher levels has minimal additional impact on the overall level of segregation or the speed with which it emerges. This is anticipated by previous studies (2, 10, 11, 12, 22) that note that, once certain critical thresholds are crossed, preferences tend to drive local areas toward homogeneity.

check.task: Put the model in a state where households ask for no more than about a third of like neighbours, yet the city is more than 65% sorted.
check.hint: Don't look for a high wish. Look for the notch near one third where one-colour patches spread across the grid.
check.misconception: Strong segregation needs strong wishes, with sorting growing step by step as households ask for more. In fact a modest wish near the threshold is already enough to sort the city strongly.

connect.caption: B_{a} is the share of like neighbours each household wants: the wish slider. B_{seg} is the segregation threshold Schelling found for two equal groups, about one third. Below the threshold the city stays near random; past it, the sorting score jumps. The rule follows the Wikipedia summary of Schelling's result; the exact threshold shifts in other variants.

concepts.recap: In Schelling-style models, sorting does not grow smoothly with what people want: it stays low at small wishes, jumps once wishes pass about one third, and then changes little.

activities.prompt: Three cities, identical except for the wish. Look at the grid and the sorting score in each.
activities.takeaway: Compare the change from a quarter to just over a third with the change from a third to a half. The sources find that the big change happens around the threshold, not steadily along the way.

concepts.title: Frozen, segregated or mixed: two settings decide together
concepts.idea: Whether the city freezes, segregates or stays mixed depends on two settings together: how many unlike neighbours households tolerate and how many homes are empty.

terms.means: The largest share of unlike neighbours a household accepts before it wants to move. Accepting at most half unlike is the same as wanting at least half alike.
The share of homes in the simulated city that are empty
A city that stays mixed because no empty home is acceptable to its households, so nobody can move
Small one-group patches scattered among many empty homes, with the two groups still kept apart

concepts.recap: Tolerance and empty homes act together: very strict freezes the city, middling segregates it, very tolerant keeps it mixed, and many empty homes thin segregation into patches.

understand.explanation: Gauvin and colleagues simulated a city in which each household caps the share of unlike neighbours it will accept, which they call its tolerance, and moves only into an empty home that meets that cap. They also varied the share of homes left empty, the vacancy density. When few homes are empty and tolerance is low, no empty home is acceptable, so nobody can move and the city stays mixed even though clusters would suit households better: a frozen state. At middle tolerance households can relocate, and the city splits into two large one-colour regions; at high tolerance almost every empty home is acceptable, the moves leave the city disordered, and it stays mixed. More empty homes lower the tolerance at which segregation appears, and at high vacancy densities the groups form many small one-colour patches in a sea of empty homes, which is dilute segregation. These are simulation results for one set of rules, mostly on a 50 by 50 grid, and the authors suggest the frozen state would probably be unstable in a more realistic model where discontented households could move to other cities.
understand.quote: For not too large values of the vacancy density there are two such transitions: At low tolerance, the system goes from a frozen state due to the dynamics that does not allow any movement, to a segregated state. At higher tolerance the system becomes mixed again.

activities.prompt: Hold the share of empty homes low and change only how tolerant households are. These three cases summarise what Gauvin and colleagues report.

cases.label: Low tolerance
cases.text: Households accept very few unlike neighbours. In the randomly mixed starting city, no empty home is acceptable to them, so they cannot move. The city stays close to how it began: mixed, with no large one-colour clusters, even though such clusters would suit the households better. This is the frozen state.

cases.label: Middle tolerance
cases.text: Now about half of the empty homes are acceptable to a given group, so households can relocate. The city separates into two large one-colour regions. In the paper's example, with 5% of homes empty and a tolerance of 0.5, the share of satisfied households was very close to 1 after about 10 time steps, and two large, convoluted clusters had already formed. The authors report that the segregated region reaches tolerances as high as 3/4.

cases.label: High tolerance
cases.text: Almost every empty home is acceptable. In this version even satisfied households can move, and when almost all moves are permitted the city ends up disordered and mixed. This mixed city differs from the frozen one: here moving is easy, not impossible.

activities.takeaway: Segregation sits in a middle band of tolerance. Very low tolerance blocks movement; very high tolerance lets moves leave the city disordered. Both ends look mixed, but for opposite reasons.

activities.prompt: Now change how many homes stand empty and see how the regions shift.

cases.label: Few empty homes
cases.text: With few vacancies, households need a relatively high tolerance before any empty home becomes acceptable. Below that, the city stays frozen.

cases.label: More empty homes (under 46%)
cases.text: The paper found that the more homes are empty, the lower the tolerance at which segregation appears and the wider the range of tolerance over which it lasts. Above 46% empty, the line between frozen and segregated no longer exists. Near that line, the same settings could end either frozen or segregated, depending on the order in which households were chosen to move.

cases.label: High share of empty homes
cases.text: At high vacancy densities, the groups are not mixed, but they form many small one-colour clusters in a sea of vacancies: dilute segregation. The switch from segregated to mixed was abrupt below 26% empty, and it became continuous at about 50% empty. Above about 56%, the authors found no clear transition: only a gradual change from dilute segregation to mixing as tolerance rises.

activities.takeaway: Neither setting decides on its own. The same tolerance can freeze, segregate or thin into scattered patches, depending on how many homes are empty.

activities.prompt: Match each pair of settings to the outcome Gauvin and colleagues report, and to the reason for it.

pairs.text: Very low tolerance, few empty homes
pairs.target: Frozen: no empty home is acceptable, so nobody moves and the city stays mixed
pairs.feedback: Right. The city looks mixed only because no move is possible, not because households want it that way.

pairs.target: Segregated: households can find acceptable homes, and the city splits into two big one-colour regions
pairs.feedback: Right. In this band about half of the empty homes are acceptable to a given group, and segregation emerges.

pairs.target: Mixed: almost every empty home is acceptable, and the moves leave the city disordered
pairs.feedback: Right. When almost all moves are permitted, the typical arrangement is a disordered, mixed one.

pairs.text: Low tolerance, a high share of empty homes (well over half)
pairs.target: Dilute segregation: many small one-colour clusters in a sea of vacancies
pairs.feedback: Right. With so many empty homes, large clusters do not form, but the two groups still do not mix.

activities.takeaway: Together these four pairs form a rough map: tolerance on one side, empty homes on the other, and a different outcome in each region.
hints: Ask first whether households can find any empty home they accept.
Very low tolerance blocks moves; very high tolerance allows almost all of them.
A very high share of empty homes stops large clusters from forming.

activities.question: A simulated city has few empty homes, and its households' tolerance is just low enough to leave it frozen. According to Gauvin and colleagues, which single change is most likely to let it segregate?

options.text: Leave more homes empty, while keeping it below 46%
options.feedback: Supported. The paper reports that as the share of empty homes rises, the frozen-to-segregated transition occurs at lower tolerance. A city just on the frozen side can cross into segregation.

options.text: Make households even less tolerant
options.feedback: Not supported. Stricter households find even fewer acceptable empty homes, so the city stays frozen.

options.text: Make households tolerate almost any mix of neighbours
options.feedback: Not supported. This overshoots. At very high tolerance almost every move is permitted and the city ends up mixed. A moderate rise in tolerance could produce segregation, but near-total tolerance skips past the segregated band.

options.text: Nothing: a frozen city can never segregate
options.feedback: Not supported. Freezing depends on the settings. Changing tolerance or the share of empty homes can move the city into the segregated region.

hints: Freezing happens because no empty home is acceptable.
How does the share of empty homes shift the tolerance at which segregation appears?

activities.question: Two simulated cities, both with few empty homes, end up looking equally mixed. One has very low tolerance and the other very high tolerance. What does the paper say about them?

options.text: They are the same: a mixed city is a mixed city
options.feedback: Not supported. The authors write that even if both final arrangements are mixed, the nature of the two states is not the same. That is why they added a second measure to tell them apart.

options.text: In the strict city no empty home is acceptable, so nobody can move; in the tolerant city almost every move is permitted, and the result is disordered
options.feedback: Supported. The paper tracked the share of empty homes a group would refuse. It is near 1 below the first transition and near 0 at high tolerance, which separates the two mixed cases.

options.text: The strict city is mixed because its households prefer diversity
options.feedback: Not supported. The paper notes that large one-colour clusters would be more satisfactory for these households. They stay mixed because they cannot reach any acceptable home.

hints: Ask whether each city's households could move if they wanted to.
One city blocks almost every move; the other permits almost every move.

activities.question: What, if anything, does the frozen state tell us about real neighbourhoods?

options.text: Strict preferences could keep a mixed neighbourhood stuck in place
options.feedback: This is a fair reading of the simulation: very low tolerance did leave the city stuck in a mixed state. Limits: it comes from one rule set on an artificial grid. Gauvin and colleagues themselves say the frozen state would probably be unstable in a more realistic model that allows discontented households to move to other cities.

options.text: It mostly reflects the model's moving rule, not people
options.feedback: This reading is well supported. The paper attributes freezing to 'the dynamics that does not allow any movement': households move only to empty homes they find acceptable. Rogers and McKane note there is no single definitive Schelling model, and variants differ in how moves are chosen. The grid model earlier in this lesson sends unhappy households to any empty home, so it does not freeze. Limit: a rule-dependent result still shows what such a rule would produce.

options.text: It proves that very prejudiced cities stay integrated
options.feedback: This goes beyond the evidence. The frozen city is mixed only because households cannot move, not because they chose integration. It is a simulation result, not an observation of real cities, and the authors suggest it would probably not last if discontented households could leave for other cities.

hints: Ask what would have to be true about real households for the freezing to happen.
Compare the moving rule here with the one in the earlier grid model.

concepts.title: When wanting outruns your group's share
concepts.idea: A group starts to segregate once the share of like neighbours its members want exceeds that group's share of the city, because then no evenly mixed neighbourhood can give them enough.

predict.question: Clark and Fossett mention a more realistic city split 65%, 25% and 10% between three groups. Suppose every household wants 30% of its neighbours to be like it. Which groups are pushed to sort by this wish, because no even mix of the city gives them enough?
options: Only the 65% group
The 25% and the 10% groups
Only the 10% group
None of them: 30% is a mild wish
why: The biggest group might seem to drive things, but an even mix gives it about 65% like neighbours, far more than the 30% it wants. It can be content in a mixed city.
Right. An even mix gives each group its own share of like neighbours: 25% and 10% both fall short of the 30% wanted, so both are pushed to gather. Only the 65% group gets enough from an even mix.
The 10% group is the furthest short, but the 25% group is short too: 25% is still less than 30%. Every group whose share is below the wish is pushed to sort.
A 30% wish is mild for a group making up 65% of the city. For a group making up 25% or 10%, even a mixed city can't deliver it. Whether a wish is mild depends on the group's share.

terms.means: The share of like neighbours a household wants before it is content where it lives
The fraction of all households in the city that belong to a given group

model.title: The same small city, now with a slider for how big each group is
model.note: Teaching model: the same 20×20 grid as before with 10% of homes empty, but the split between the two groups can now be changed. Only unhappy households move, and each jumps to a random empty home. Each household looks only at its eight neighbouring homes. Clark and Fossett used a richer simulation (SimSeg) with three groups, neighbourhoods of 40 nearby homes, and households that also cared about housing quality and income. This two-group grid is a simplified stand-in for their central result. The score averages over all households, so when one group is small, the big group dominates it. That is why the model also shows the score a random mix would give. With only eight neighbours, the mix around each home varies a lot, so sorting here can begin a little below a group's share rather than exactly at it. Numbers are illustrative, not the sources' data.

Share of households in group A

steps.say: This is the same city as before: two colours of households on a grid, a slider for how many like neighbours each wants, and one for how many rounds run.
New: this slider sets how much of the city belongs to group A. Watch the grid as group A shrinks to a fifth of all households.
And a new yardstick: the same-group share you'd get by pure chance in a random mix. With a small group, it is no longer 50%.

explore.prompt: Use group size to make a mild wish bite. Try different splits and compare the score with what a random mix would give.

goals.text: Keep each household's wish at 25% or lower, but change the size of the groups so that one group is short of like neighbours and the city sorts clearly beyond a random mix.
hints: Which group gets too few like neighbours in a random mix: a big one or a small one?
Keep the wish low and move the group-A slider. In a random mix, a household's like neighbours roughly match its group's share of the city.
Make one group's share smaller than the wish setting, then check that the score sits well above the random-mix line.

feedback.correct: Yes. An even mix gives every group exactly its own share of like neighbours. Any group whose share is below the wish (here the 25% and 10% groups) can't be satisfied by mixing, so it is pushed to gather.
feedback.incorrect: It is tempting to judge a wish as mild or strong on its own. The idea compares it with each group's share of the city: an even mix hands each group its share of like neighbours, so every group whose share is below the wish (25% and 10% here) is pushed to sort.

steps.say: Start where the last lesson found a calm city: two equal halves, each household wanting 20% like neighbours. The score sits only a little above its random-mix level.
Same mild wish, but now group A is just 15 households in every 100. Look at the grid: group A's households start to bunch together.

First, a fair yardstick. With one small group, big-group households are mostly surrounded by their own kind even in a random mix. So the random-mix level is now well above 50%, and the gain line measures sorting beyond it.
Why does group A sort? In a random mix, about 15% of an A household's neighbours are A, its share of the city. It wants 20%. An evenly mixed neighbourhood simply can't give it enough, so it moves.

Let's name the two numbers. The share a household wants is its preference target. The share of the city its group makes up is the group's population share. Sorting is pushed along once the target is above the share.
Now make group A the big one. Group B is the 15% group now, short of its 20% target, and B's households bunch up instead. What matters is the smaller group's share.

A wrinkle: with only eight neighbours, the mix near each home varies, so sorting here can start below a group's share. The equal city tipped near a third. Clark and Fossett's 40-home neighbourhoods put the jump near the share.

understand.explanation: In an evenly mixed city, a household can expect its share of like neighbours to equal its group's share of the city. If a group's members want more than that, no evenly mixed neighbourhood gives them enough, so they move and gather, and sorting follows. That is why a wish that left two equal halves mixed sorts a city where one group is small. Clark and Fossett showed this with their SimSeg simulations of three equal groups (about a third each), where households looked at 40 nearby homes and also cared about housing quality and income: segregation stayed low when households wanted 20% like neighbours and rose to high levels at 40%. They also note that more realistic, unequal sizes such as 65%, 25% and 10% gave even more segregation. Two caveats: with only eight neighbours, this small grid can start sorting somewhat below a group's share, and any simulation shows what preferences could produce, not what real cities actually do.
understand.quote: The crucial transition occurs when preference targets reach or exceed a group's population representation (22). Thus, high levels of segregation emerge when targets for same-group contact shift from 20% to 40%. Segregation is low when households seek 20% same-group contact because all households can be satisfied in neighborhoods that match the city's ethnic mix.

connect.caption: This is the lesson's statement of Clark and Fossett's rule, which they give in words, not as an equation. T (coloured like the wish slider) is the preference target: the share of like neighbours wanted. p_{small} is the smaller group's population share, set by the group-A slider p_{A}. An even mix gives each group its own share of like neighbours, so the group is short whenever T is above its share. The random-mix yardstick in the model is p_{A}² + (1 − p_{A})².

concepts.recap: A group is pushed to sort once it wants more like neighbours than its share of the city, because an even mix can only ever give it its share.

activities.title: Could an even mix satisfy them?
activities.prompt: Each card describes a group and the share of like neighbours its members want. In an evenly mixed city, each group's like neighbours match its share of the city. Sort each card by whether that is enough.

groups.label: An evenly mixed city gives them enough
No evenly mixed city gives them enough

cards.text: Two equal halves; everyone wants 20% like neighbours.
cards.feedback: An even mix gives each household about 50% like neighbours, well above the 20% wanted.

cards.text: Three equal groups, a third each; everyone wants 20%.
cards.feedback: A third is more than 20%. This mirrors Clark and Fossett's case where segregation stayed low.

cards.text: Three equal groups, a third each; everyone wants 40%.
cards.feedback: 40% is more than a third, so even a perfect mix leaves everyone short. In Clark and Fossett's simulations, high segregation emerged here.

cards.text: A group that is 10% of the city; members want at least 3 of their 8 neighbours to be like them.
cards.feedback: 3 of 8 is 37.5%, far above the 10% an even mix would give.

cards.text: A group that is 70% of the city; members want half their neighbours to be like them.
cards.feedback: An even mix gives this group about 70% like neighbours, more than the half it wants.

cards.text: A group that is 25% of the city; members want half their neighbours to be like them.
cards.feedback: An even mix gives only about 25% like neighbours, half of what is wanted.

cards.text: A group that is 40% of the city; members want 30%.
cards.feedback: On average an even mix gives 40%, above the 30% wanted. With small neighbourhoods, though, chance variation can still leave some households short.

activities.takeaway: Compare the wish with the group's share of the city, not with some fixed idea of a mild wish. 'Enough' only means an even mix could work on average: in small neighbourhoods, chance variation can still set off some sorting.

concepts.title: More segregated than anyone wanted
concepts.idea: Households content to be a one-third minority still end up surrounded mostly by their own group, so the city is far more segregated than any individual asked for; this shows that preferences could produce segregation, not that they do.

predict.question: Picture a new town. Most households want about a third of their neighbours to be like them. A sizeable minority are far more open and would happily be one of very few of their kind. Following the sources' argument, what happens to the open households and the town?
options: The town still sorts, and the open households end up living in sorted neighbourhoods too
The open households settle in mixed areas and keep those areas mixed
The town ends up exactly halfway between the two groups' wishes
The most open households decide the outcome for everyone
why: Correct. Clark and Fossett argue that the most tolerant members don't set the outcome. Each arrival makes an area more attractive to the newcomer's own group, so areas drift toward sameness, and the open households end up there too.
It is tempting to think open households can hold mixed areas together. But everyone else's moves keep pulling each area toward one group, and the open households have no reason to leave.
It sounds fair to average the wishes. But moves feed on each other, so the city overshoots the wishes rather than landing between them.
One very open household doesn't set the pattern. The result comes from everyone's moves interacting, not from any single household's choice.

terms.means: The pattern of the whole city, such as how sorted it is, as opposed to what each household wants
Separation that comes about through people's choices and moves, not because a law or rule requires it

model.title: The same small city, now comparing what households wanted with what they got
model.note: Teaching model: the same 20×20 grid as before, with two equal groups and 10% of homes empty. Only unhappy households move, and each jumps to a random empty home. Schelling moved them to the nearest home that would satisfy them. The score averages, over all households, the share of occupied neighbouring homes (up to eight) that hold the household's own group. The new box, result minus wish, is this lesson's own measure, not one the sources use. A wish of about a third means being content with 3 like neighbours out of 8, a minority. Real survey wishes reported by Clark and Fossett are higher, around 40–60%, and their simulations used three groups, housing quality and income; this model leaves all of that out. Numbers are illustrative, not the sources' data.

This is the score you know: on average, what share of a household's neighbours are from its own group.
New here: this box subtracts what each household asked for from what it ended up with. A big number means the city went far past anyone's wish.

explore.prompt: Now try it yourself: find mild wishes that still leave the city heavily sorted, and watch how far the result runs past the wish.

goals.text: Give households a wish mild enough that they would accept being outnumbered by their neighbours, yet still end with at least three in five of their neighbours from their own group, on average
hints: Too mild, and almost nobody moves. Too strong, and households no longer accept being outnumbered.
Think back to where the city tipped in the earlier lesson. The wish has to sit on the sorting side of that point but stay below half. Give the computer plenty of rounds to settle.
Out of eight neighbours, being outnumbered but content means being fine with three like neighbours. Pick the lowest slider setting that asks for exactly that.

goals.text: Make the city end up at least 25 points more sorted than households asked for, while it is also clearly sorted, at least 10 points above a random mix
hints: A tiny wish makes the result-minus-wish box large, but is the city actually sorted then? Check the box for sorting above a random mix.
A random mix already gives about 50% like neighbours. The wish must be strong enough to tip the city and still leave a lot of room above it.
Look just past the tipping point you found in the earlier lesson, not far above it.

feedback.correct: Yes. Outcomes come from everyone's moves interacting, not from the most tolerant members. Each arrival makes an area more attractive to the newcomer's own group, so areas drift toward sameness, and open-minded households end up in sorted areas too.
feedback.incorrect: You probably expected the outcome to mirror what people want, either an average of the wishes or the most open households' wishes. In Schelling-style dynamics, moves feed on each other, so the city overshoots the wishes. Even very open households end up in sorted neighbourhoods.

steps.say: Start with almost no wish: households only mind being nearly alone among the other group. Very few move, and the score stays near 50%, the level of a random mix.
Now set a wish of about a third. In everyday terms, each household is content with 3 like neighbours out of 8. It would happily live outnumbered, 5 to 3.
Look at the result. The average household now has most of its neighbours from its own group, well over half, not the third it asked for.
This box measures the overshoot: tens of points of sorting that nobody asked for. Compare it with the sorting-above-random box to see that this is real sorting, not the random starting mix.
And few or no households are left unhappy. Nobody's wish was broken. Each got what it wanted, and the moves of everyone together delivered far more.
The sorted city is a macro outcome: a pattern of the whole city that no single household chose. No law forced it, so it is de facto segregation.
A caution: the model shows that mild preferences could produce this. It does not show that real cities sorted this way, or that sorted cities hold prejudiced people.
So here is the punchline. Households happy to be a one-third minority still end up in a city where most neighbours are just like them, far more segregated than anyone asked for.

understand.explanation: Even when every household would gladly be outnumbered, about 3 like neighbours out of 8, the city ends up with most people living mainly among their own group. Each move makes the old area less attractive to the mover's group and the new area less attractive to the other group, so neighbourhoods drift toward sameness. Schelling showed this with hand-run simulations. Clark and Fossett repeated it with a richer simulation that used three groups, income and housing quality, and wishes set at levels found in surveys. Segregation rose quickly and stayed high, more than most households would call ideal. But the authors frame this as a test of what preferences can do, not proof of what happened in real cities. Real data cannot separate preferences from discrimination and income gaps, and these likely act together.
understand.quote: Unless most households are strongly averse to majority status—and surveys indicate this is not the case, local neighborhoods will drift toward ethnic homogeneity. The resulting neighborhood structure is more segregated than most individual households would find “ideal.”

check.question: A student watches this model turn mild wishes into a highly sorted city. Then they read that a real city is highly segregated. Which conclusion is justified?

options.text: The real city's residents must be strongly prejudiced, because sorting this strong needs strong dislike.
options.why: The model shows the opposite: mild wishes are enough to produce strong sorting. A sorted outcome tells you little about how strong anyone's wishes are.

options.text: Mild preferences could be enough to produce that pattern, but the model alone can't say whether they did. Discrimination, income gaps and history may also be at work, possibly together.
options.why: This matches the sources: the models show preferences have the logical capacity to produce segregation, while real causes are hard to separate and likely combine.

options.text: The real city's segregation was caused by preferences, not by discrimination.
options.why: A model reproducing a pattern shows one possible cause, not the actual one. Clark and Fossett stress that the factors are not mutually exclusive and that nonexperimental data make them hard to separate.

options.text: If residents report only mild wishes, their choices can't be what keeps the city segregated.
options.why: This is exactly what the model refutes: mild wishes, acted on by everyone, can still leave a city heavily sorted.

check.hint: Ask two separate questions: what does the outcome say about individuals' wishes, and can a model that reproduces a pattern say what caused it in a real city?
check.misconception: That a segregated city reveals strongly prejudiced residents, or that a model which reproduces segregation proves what caused it in a real city.

connect.caption: The rule is Schelling's, in the notation of the Wikipedia summary. B is the share of a household's neighbours from its own group, and B_{a} (blue, the wish slider) is the share it wants; it moves while B < B_{a}. ⟨B⟩ (the sorting score) is the city-wide average of B after the moves. The overshoot ⟨B⟩ − B_{a} is this lesson's own measure, not one the sources define. It comes out large even though every household only asked for B_{a}.

concepts.recap: Mild wishes, acted on by everyone, can sort a city far beyond what anyone asked for. That shows preferences could cause segregation, not that they did.
